children: As JSW expands beyond the industrial businesses built around steel, Parth Jindal is overseeing very different bets in paint, automobiles and other areas. These businesses, he says, grew from opportunities identified along the way rather than a single grand plan. In conversation with BW Businessworld’s Group Editorial Director, Noor Fathima Warsia, he discusses how they emerged, what it will take to make them pay, and why the group must eventually outgrow dependence on the family
JSW has expanded into several new businesses. Could any of them eventually rival steel in scale and importance?

Steel will remain our biggest business for at least the next few years. But if any business can challenge it within the group, it is automobiles, because of its size, scale and ambition. Consumer businesses are still early days for us, and they need a different set of professionals from the B2B businesses we know. We have built those teams, and I think people are attracted when the mission is larger than the business.

In electric vehicles, my father’s view is that India needs to become more self-sufficient. We import oil and make our own power, so electric mobility can improve energy security and bring environmental benefits. People also know JSW as a manufacturing group that can build at scale. That combination helps us attract the people we need. I see diversification as a strength.
How are you building the automobile business, and where do the different partnerships fit?

New energy vehicles are a large opportunity, but automobiles are a scale business. We have MG through our joint venture with SAIC. We plan to launch the separate JSW Motors passenger vehicle brand in December 2026 under a licensing arrangement with Chery. We are building an electric bus and truck business too. And we are in discussions with Škoda Volkswagen.

That could potentially add another passenger vehicle brand, but it is still a conversation. We think the Rs 10 lakh to Rs 20 lakh range is the sweet spot for the shift to electric. There is a larger purpose too. India imports oil but makes its own power. Electrification can improve our energy security and bring environmental benefits. Our ambition is to sell close to a million passenger new energy vehicles a year, perhaps by 2030 or 2032. We are building capacity towards that ambition.

We plan to launch the separate JSW Motors passenger vehicle brand in December 2026 under a licensing arrangement with Chery. We are building an electric bus and truck business too. And we are in discussions with Škoda Volkswagen"
Would two passenger vehicle brands under your influence compete with each other?

I want MG to push JSW and JSW to push MG. To the customer, they should offer choice, different models and platforms, with each brand competing for the sale. Behind the scenes, the scale can work together. If we combine the requirements of both businesses when we talk to component, battery, seat or glass suppliers, we can get better costs. That should let us offer better prices. The front end is competition, the back end is where we seek economies of scale.
MG is still loss-making. What turns it into a profitable manufacturer?

Localisation is the key, and it has been a steep learning curve. Before we came in, MG imported most components and assembled vehicles in India. The Windsor, launched in October 2024, began with localisation in the low double digits. Our roadmap is to reach roughly 65 to 70 per cent by the end of calendar 2027.

It takes 18 to 24 months to localise a product, and different components move at different speeds. When you import parts, you buy in dollars and sell in rupees. The exchange rate and freight costs affect you. Local production gives you more control. We expect calendar 2027 to be MG’s first profitable year and calendar 2028 for JSW Motors. These are targets, and we are taking the lessons from MG into the new business.
"Localisation is the key, and it has been a steep learning curve"
Why buy Akzo Nobel India when you had already built JSW Paints?

We entered paint in 2019 and built a sizeable business, but we faced two challenges. In decorative paint, people knew JSW for steel and cement, not necessarily for the walls of their homes. Building that trust organically would have taken substantial spending. In industrial coatings, approvals from carmakers, marine customers and other equipment makers can take three or four years.

About 70 per cent of our early industrial sales went to companies in the wider O.P. Jindal group. It was much harder to break into other customers. Akzo Nobel India gave us Dulux, a recognised paint brand, along with distribution, products, people and industrial approvals. We also have access to AkzoNobel’s continuing research through a licence for industrial formulations, for which we pay a 4.5 per cent royalty. It addressed barriers on both sides of the business much faster than we could have on our own.
How will you keep Dulux and JSW Paints distinct, and when does the acquisition earn its keep?

Dulux should lead in premium decorative paint -- walls, wood finishes, wallpaper and painting services. JSW should lead in value products, waterproofing, putty and construction chemicals. We hope to merge JSW Paints into JSW Dulux in 2027, while keeping those brand roles distinct.

The aim is to be among the top three or four in decorative paint and number one in industrial coatings. My father questioned why we should commit so much to an acquisition instead of investing more in JSW Paints. I explained the logic, and everyone eventually agreed. We see this as a three-to-five-year effort to build a meaningful business. If everything goes well, I expect significant returns for the group by 2030.
Sport is a very different undertaking for JSW. What has it meant to the group and to you?

There is nothing that brings a country together like sport. Our work in Indian Olympic sport over the past 13 years has shown our employees that the group thinks about India, not just itself. It has built recognition for JSW, but it has also helped me understand India better. We do social work through sport and through the foundation, and there is a business side as well. As India becomes more affluent, people will spend more on sport. That is already beginning, though there is a long way to go. I am excited about both sides of it.
Some JSW businesses connect with one another, while others stand apart. Do you see them as an ecosystem? And which business could go public next?

I would look at them as separate businesses. Defence is an example. We saw an opportunity to manufacture drones for the Indian armed forces, so we invested in JSW Defence. That requires manufacturing capability and the ability to work with government, but it has no real link to paint, cars or the rest of the group. I founded the business, but I do not run it day to day. I only review it monthly, as the team runs it.

We intend to take businesses public when they reach sufficient size and scale. A listing gives them capital to grow faster. Auto could go public in time, and we hope to list JSW One in 2027. Defence is too small for us to contemplate a listing today.
How do you make sure the family’s new investments do not burden existing listed companies?

The risk comes when a family leverages one business to grow another. That is when the interests become blurred. Dividends paid to the family are our money, and we can decide whether to reinvest them or incubate a new business. We are not putting debt on one existing business to finance a new one. Each company must reach the point where it can fund its growth and, if needed, raise capital itself through a QIP or bonds.
"The group cannot be dependent on the family now"
You oversee several businesses. How do you want leadership to work as JSW grows?

The group cannot be dependent on the family now. Each business needs a solid management team, a solid board and independent directors. I am proud to have contributed to professionalising the group over the past decade. Today my father and I are involved because we enjoy it and believe we add value. Ten years from now, a single family cannot be responsible for running something of this size. We will remain shareholders and can serve on boards. If the next generation wants an operating role and is capable, great. If not, it should not have one. The group has to become an institution. Growing up, we admired the way the Tata group had grown and professionalised. That has been our mission too.
What should JSW stand for in the coming years?

Manufacturing excellence. We want Indian consumers to think of technology, quality and Atmanirbharta when they hear JSW. We should be able to bring technology from anywhere, localise it and make products to world standards in India, for India and for the world.

We are a $25 billion revenue group and plan to invest close to $58 billion over the next five years across our businesses. If India grows at seven to eight per cent annually, our ambition should be to grow three times as fast. That is the scale of what we are setting out to do.
